opus-5.5.text:
I think mixture-of-experts is one of the more interesting directions we have, but it's worth being precise about what kind of specialization it actually gives you.

The appeal is intuitive. Instead of activating every parameter for every input, you route each token to a subset of experts. You decouple total capacity from compute per example, so you can grow the model without paying the full inference cost each time. From an efficiency standpoint that's very compelling, and it fits a theme I care about: we shouldn't treat every input as if it needs the entire network.

Where I get more cautious is the word "specialization." When people inspect what the experts learn in practice, it's often not the clean semantic division you might hope for. You don't reliably get a math expert, a code expert, and a French expert. Routing often picks up shallower patterns, like token-level or syntactic features. So yes, the experts are specialized in some sense, but not necessarily in a way that's interpretable or that maps onto the tasks we care about.

There are also real practical challenges. Training is less stable. You need load-balancing losses so a few experts don't get all the traffic while others collapse. Serving is harder, because memory footprint still scales with total parameters even if compute doesn't, and that matters a lot if you care about access. Much of the world isn't running on large clusters.

Our group has also been interested in making MoE more parameter-efficient. For example, we've looked at combining the mixture idea with lightweight adapters, so the experts are small modules rather than full feed-forward blocks. That keeps the benefits of conditional computation without exploding the parameter count, and it can work well for instruction tuning and adapting to new tasks.

So my overall view is that MoE is a very useful tool for conditional compute and efficiency, and it's part of a broader shift away from purely dense scaling. But I'd be careful about assuming it delivers true modular specialization automatically. If we want experts that really specialize, whether by language, domain, or capability, we probably need more deliberate choices about routing, data, and how we merge or compose those experts. I think that's where many of the open research questions are.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think mixture-of-experts is really interesting, and I'd actually situate it in a longer history of ideas about how we allocate capacity. If you go back to the early nineties, Jacobs and Jordan and Hinton were already thinking about adaptive mixtures of local experts, so this is not a new idea. What's new is the scale and the engineering around it, and I think that's where a lot of the excitement comes from, because it gives you a way to decouple the number of parameters from the compute you spend per token.

But I think it's worth being precise about what "specialization" means here, because the word gets used in a way that implies something it often doesn't deliver. The intuition people have is that one expert becomes the "code expert," another the "French expert," and so on, and that's a very clean story. When you actually look at routing behavior, it tends to be much messier. Experts often specialize on fairly low-level features, things like token position, punctuation, syntactic patterns, rather than the semantic categories we'd like to see. So the specialization is real, but it's not necessarily the kind of specialization that's interpretable or that maps onto how we'd want to carve up the world.

The second thing I'd say is that MoE is really an efficiency story more than a capability story. The gains are in inference cost and training throughput for a given quality level. That matters enormously, particularly if you care about who gets to deploy these models and at what cost. But it also means you inherit a lot of complexity: load balancing, routing collapse where a few experts get all the traffic, instability during training, and the memory footprint, because you still have to hold all those parameters somewhere even if you're only activating a fraction. So the sparsity helps you on FLOPs but doesn't help you nearly as much on memory, which for a lot of real deployment settings is the actual constraint.

And then the thing I care a lot about, which is the multilingual and long-tail setting, I think is where MoE gets both most interesting and most fragile. In principle, having more capacity that can be routed conditionally is exactly what you want when you have very heterogeneous data, where some languages or domains are massively underrepresented. In practice, the router is trained on the same skewed distribution as everything else, so there's a risk that the long tail gets squeezed into whatever experts are left over, and you reproduce the same inequities you had in a dense model, just with an extra layer of indirection. We've seen with things like the lottery of which capabilities survive compression that it's always the rare examples that are hit first, and I don't think MoE is automatically immune to that.

So my overall assessment is that it's a very pragmatic and increasingly standard tool, and I think it's going to remain part of the frontier recipe. But I'd push back on the framing of it as a route to specialization in the way people often mean. If what you want is genuine modularity, where you can add a capability, remove one, update one part of the model without touching everything else, I think we're still quite far from that, and MoE as it's currently practiced is more of an engineering trick that borrows the language of modularity than a realization of it. The more exciting direction for me is thinking about how you make that modularity real, whether that's through more deliberate expert design, through composing separately trained components, or through rethinking how we represent and route to knowledge at all.

astra-6.text:
I think mixture-of-experts models are a promising way to increase capacity without activating every parameter for every input. But I’d distinguish that from specialization in the sense that we usually mean it.

Calling something an “expert” suggests that one component understands medicine and another understands law. The architecture doesn’t necessarily give you that. You have a routing mechanism that learns to send inputs to different parts of the model, and the resulting division of work may not map neatly onto domains or skills that a human would recognize.

So the question is: what kind of specialization do you want, and how would you measure it? If you want computational efficiency, you can look at quality relative to the amount of computation used. If you want expertise in a particular domain, you need to evaluate that directly. You also need to understand whether routing actually helps on less common inputs, rather than simply reinforcing the patterns that dominate training.

For me, it’s an interesting architectural mechanism, but the name alone doesn’t establish that you’ve achieved meaningful specialization.

sol-6.1.text:
I think mixture-of-experts models are a useful direction, but I’d be careful about equating the word “expert” with specialization. Architecturally, you have different sets of parameters, and a router decides which ones to activate for a given input. That gives you a way to increase model capacity without activating all of those parameters for every token.

But that doesn’t necessarily mean one expert becomes great at medicine and another becomes great at law. The specialization that emerges may be much less intuitive, and it depends on the training objective and the routing mechanism. You also have this tension between letting experts differentiate and making sure the router doesn’t send everything to just a few of them.

So I’d separate two questions: Is this an effective way to allocate computation? And does it produce meaningful specialization that we can understand and control? I’m optimistic about the first. On the second, I think we need to look carefully at what the experts actually learn, rather than infer it from the architecture’s name.
